preamble: Deaffrication of the voiced alveolar affricate [dz] to the fricative [z], through loss of the stop closure. It happened independently in medieval Romance (Old French, Galician-Portuguese and Old Spanish all lost their dental affricates) and in most Slavic languages, where the [dz] produced by the second and third palatalizations of *g became [z] everywhere except Polish, Slovak and early Old Church Slavonic.

examples.note: The affricates /ts dz tʃ dʒ/ became the fricatives [s z ʃ ʒ] by Middle French; Old French wrote /dz/ as z.
Portuguese, like Old Spanish, deaffricated /ts/ and /dz/ to lamino-alveolar fricatives, later merged with the apical ones in most dialects.

examples.from: Proto-Slavic *kъnędzь 'prince'; Old Church Slavonic кънѧѕь kŭnędzĭ
examples.to: Russian князь knjazʹ; also OCS кънѧзь kŭnęzĭ
examples.note: The *dz from the third palatalization became z; Polish ksiądz keeps the affricate. Czech kněz and Serbo-Croatian knȇz show the same z.

languageExamples.language: Proto-Central Chadic North to Proto-Kotoko Centre (Lagwan, Mser)

examples.note: Gravina pairs this with *ts → s: both affricates became fricatives in the Kotoko Centre group.
The Kotoko Centre and Gidar changes are independent; the Musgum group instead has *dz → d.

sources: Gravina, R. (2014). The Phonology of Proto-Central Chadic: The Reconstruction of the Phonology and Lexicon of Proto-Central Chadic, and the Linguistic History of the Central Chadic Languages. https://www.lotpublications.nl/Documents/375_fulltext.pdf
